strengths: Significance: PersistBench addresses an important practical problem: distinguishing useful personalization from inappropriate use of stored user information. Including 200 leakage, 200 sycophancy, and 100 beneficial-memory cases makes the benchmark potentially useful for evaluating safety–utility trade-offs.

Originality: The contribution is a useful evaluation perspective combining memory-conditioned sycophancy, cross-domain interference, and beneficial memory use. Its value lies primarily in this benchmark formulation and empirical characterization rather than a new algorithm.

Soundness: Evaluation across 18 models is substantial. The memory-disabled control across all 200 sycophancy cases for five models supports the claim that the supplied memories increase measured failures. Memory swapping, query paraphrasing, human screening, and judge validation provide additional supporting evidence.

Presentation and limitations: The main setup is understandable, and the appendices provide extensive examples, model-level results, and FR@1/FR@2/FR@3 comparisons. The authors acknowledge synthetic-data and upstream-memory-construction limitations. Synthetic profiles reduce direct privacy concerns; no material ethical violation is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness—utility scoring is internally inconsistent. Section 4.3 defines beneficial-memory scores as 1 for correct use and 3 for no relevant use, counting scores ≥2 as failures. Appendix O.4.3 instead defines 3 as perfect and 1 as failure. Appendix Q.3 follows the main-text convention. An undocumented score reversal may explain this, but the submitted description does not establish which implementation produced the utility results. This directly affects the central safety–utility comparisons.

Soundness—judge error is material to the headline metric. Appendix E reports approximately 78% binary accuracy for both safety categories. Figure 11 shows 8 false positives among 32 human-labeled acceptable leakage responses; Figure 13 shows 5 among 19 acceptable sycophancy responses. Counting any positive judgment across three responses can amplify false positives. The paper does not validate the resulting sample-level FR@3 against humans or incorporate evaluator uncertainty into its confidence intervals. Calling over-flagging preferable for safety does not establish accurate benchmark measurement.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a benchmark-centered contribution. The code link after Section 4.3 and the 'Full prompt source' entries in Appendix O are blank. Appendix O explicitly supplies summaries rather than complete prompts, and Appendix C.1 postpones dataset release until publication. Target-model sampling temperatures, output limits, and complete version/settings information are also missing despite the reproducibility statement. Consequently, readers cannot reproduce the reported evaluation or resolve the scoring inconsistency.

The results support an adversarial stress test more strongly than the broad deployment claims. MCTS optimizes cases for failures, and validation retains cases that fail additional models. Several evaluated models participated in construction; moreover, MiniMax-M2 appears in both sycophancy search and validation, contradicting the claim that validation models were unused during generation. Appendix I's assertion that these entries represent the broader target domain is not established. Headline rates should be explicitly framed as FR@3 on selected adversarial cases, with separate reporting for construction-exposed and fully held-out models.

Construct validity needs stronger adjudication. Each benchmark item receives only one human screening judgment, while the measured distinction between inappropriate influence and useful personalization is sometimes debatable. For example, the art-history cousin example in Appendix Q.1 receives a failure score despite extensive relevant advice, principally because it suggests drawing on the user's creative background. Independent adjudication of borderline cases, especially around the failure threshold, would make the benchmark more reliable.

The defense conclusions lack a clearly independent evaluation. GEPA uses 20 examples per category, while Appendix J evaluates 50 examples per category subsampled from the benchmark; overlap is not specified. Optimization budget and configuration are insufficiently documented, and uncertainty for the claimed Pareto improvements is absent. These results do not yet establish generalizable mitigation gains.

Scope and presentation overstate what is established. Static memory injection evaluates inference-time context use, not actual persistence, forgetting, or end-to-end memory management. Appendix P tests alternative system prompts only for leakage on two models, which is insufficient for the broad claim that both failures are consistent across prompts. The work provides credible evidence of a useful problem, but unresolved measurement and reproducibility issues prevent accepting its quantitative benchmark claims as currently presented.

strengths: Significance: Evaluating inappropriate memory use alongside beneficial personalization addresses a useful problem for conversational assistants. The 100 beneficial-memory examples help prevent treating universal memory suppression as a satisfactory solution.

Originality: The contribution is principally a benchmark and empirical characterization, combining cross-domain leakage, memory-induced sycophancy, and utility. This is a meaningful extension beyond evaluating memory recall alone.

Soundness: The evaluation covers 18 models and includes substantive controls. In Appendix L, removing memories reduces sycophancy substantially across five models on all 200 examples, supporting the narrower conclusion that these memory profiles amplify the measured behavior. Memory swapping, paraphrasing, and defensive-prompt experiments provide additional evidence.

Presentation: The main experimental setup is understandable, and the appendices provide extensive examples, judge-validation results, and FR@1/FR@2 results that help interpret the headline FR@3 metric.

Limitations and ethics: The paper acknowledges synthetic-data limitations and its focus on inference-time memory use. Synthetic profiles reduce concerns about exposing real users' sensitive information; no material ethical violation is evident from the manuscript.
weaknesses: Soundness—construct validity: Some examples do not establish that the remembered information is irrelevant or the preference objectively incorrect. Appendix N.1.1 treats a deep-water phobia as inappropriate context for recommending deep-sea documentaries, although it could reasonably affect recommendations. Appendix N.2.1 treats preferring asynchronous summaries over daily stand-ups as a sycophancy scenario without establishing a uniquely correct workflow. These cases require clearer boundaries between harmful agreement, reasonable preference adaptation, and excessive flattery. Single-annotator verification of each benchmark item does not resolve this ambiguity.

Soundness—measurement reliability: Appendix E reports approximately 78% binary judge accuracy for both safety categories. The confusion matrices show false-positive rates of 8/32 for leakage and 5/19 for sycophancy; leakage precision is only 68%. These are consequential errors when the headline metric counts any judged failure across three generations. High one-point agreement does not establish threshold reliability because a one-point difference can change the failure label. Larger, model-stratified human audits and sensitivity analyses are needed before trusting precise failure rates and rankings.

Soundness—interpretation of failure rates: MCTS explicitly searches for failures, and validation retains challenging examples. This is appropriate for a stress test, but it does not estimate ordinary deployment prevalence. The abstract's headline percentages additionally represent failure in at least one of three attempts, whereas beneficial-memory failures use one attempt. Appendix H usefully reports single-attempt results, but the headline framing and safety–utility comparisons need clearer qualification. Appendix I's claims of population representativeness are not justified by bootstrapping adaptively selected examples.

Reproducibility: Section 4.3 ends with an empty code-availability reference, and Appendix O supplies prompt summaries followed by blank 'Full prompt source' fields. Appendix C promises release upon publication, but the supplied manuscript does not provide the benchmark or complete evaluation prompts. Target-model sampling temperatures and token limits are also unspecified. These omissions are material for reproducing stochastic FR@3 results and assessing the benchmark itself.

Presentation and metric consistency: Section 4.3 defines beneficial-memory score 1 as success and score 3 as failure, while Appendices G and O.4.3 reverse that orientation. Appendix Q again uses 1 for successful integration. An undocumented score transformation could explain this, but the manuscript must explicitly reconcile the rubric, aggregation code, and reported results. Section 5.1 also says 14 models exceed 95% sycophancy failure, whereas Table 2 shows 12.

Experimental separation: Appendix C.2.2 lists MiniMax-M2 in both generation and validation, contradicting the claim that all three validation models were unused during generation. For GEPA, the paper specifies 20 optimization examples per category and 50 evaluation examples per category but does not establish disjointness or provide sufficient optimization details. Consequently, the defense results cannot yet establish held-out improvement.

Significance and claim scope: The experiments establish vulnerabilities under injected textual profiles, but do not isolate persistence itself from ordinary contextual influence or evaluate memory extraction, retrieval, updating, or forgetting. The generic-system-prompt ablation covers only two models and cross-domain leakage, so it cannot support broad robustness claims across both failure categories. The scoped benchmark remains useful, but unresolved validity and reproducibility issues prevent acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Significance: Evaluating inappropriate memory use alongside beneficial personalization addresses a useful and timely problem. The 500-example benchmark and evaluation of 18 models provide a substantial starting point for studying selective memory use.

Originality: The joint treatment of cross-domain leakage, memory-conditioned sycophancy, and memory utility offers a useful evaluation perspective beyond recall accuracy. The contribution is primarily benchmark design and empirical understanding.

Soundness: The memory-disabled control provides meaningful evidence of memory amplification: across five models, sycophancy falls from 59–100% with memory to 19–38% without it (Appendix L). Memory-swapping and paraphrasing experiments offer additional support, and Appendix H transparently reports single-generation failure rates.

Presentation and transparency: The central setup is understandable, and the appendices document construction stages, qualitative examples, judge validation, and model-specific defense results. Reporting imperfect human–judge agreement is valuable.

Limitations and ethics: The paper acknowledges synthetic-data limitations and its focus on inference-time memory use. Synthetic profiles avoid directly exposing real users’ conversation histories; no material ethical violation is apparent from the manuscript.
weaknesses: Soundness—construct validity: Several examples blur harmful influence with legitimate personalization. Appendix N.1.1 treats a remembered fear of deep water as irrelevant to deep-sea documentary recommendations and describes the shared meaning of 'deep' as a polysemous lexical bridge. Appendix N.2.1 treats preferences for asynchronous summaries over stand-ups as an example of supposedly incorrect expert beliefs, although this is context-dependent. These examples undermine the claim that queries uniformly require objective, belief-independent answers. Independent annotation should distinguish factual distortion, inappropriate disclosure, excessive validation, and reasonable preference adaptation.

Soundness—measurement uncertainty: Appendix E reports only about 78% binary judge accuracy, with 68% precision for leakage, based on 52 leakage and 50 sycophancy examples. Taking any judge-positive response among three generations can amplify false positives. Ordinal agreement and one-point accuracy do not resolve errors across the decisive 2/3 threshold. The headline rates and rankings need a larger, model-stratified human audit and sensitivity analysis incorporating judge error; the bootstrap intervals currently capture only sample variation.

Reproducibility: The submitted manuscript has a blank codebase link and blank 'Full prompt source' entries. Appendix O explicitly provides prompt summaries rather than complete prompts, and target-model decoding settings are not adequately specified. Furthermore, Appendix O.4.3 defines beneficial-memory score 3 as success and score 1 as failure, reversing Section 4.3 and the examples without documenting a conversion. These gaps prevent verification of the reported utility results and exact replication of the benchmark.

Scope and statistical interpretation: Failure-seeking MCTS and subsequent failure-based filtering produce an adversarial stress test, not a representative estimate of deployed-assistant risk. Appendix I nevertheless asserts representativeness of a broader target domain from an insufficiently justified i.i.d. assumption. Some evaluated models also participate in construction or filtering, and MiniMax-M2 appears in both the sycophancy search and supposedly held-out validation sets. Results should distinguish construction models from genuinely held-out models and limit population-level conclusions. Static context injection establishes vulnerability to supplied profiles, but does not by itself establish a mechanism specific to persistence across sessions.

Defense evidence and presentation: GEPA uses 20 examples per category, while defense evaluation uses 50 per category; their disjointness is not stated. Without a documented held-out split and uncertainty estimates, the claimed Pareto advantage remains provisional. The text also overstates some results: Section 5.1 claims 14 models exceed 95% sycophancy failure, whereas Table 2 shows 12. Overall, the useful research direction and extensive experiments do not yet overcome the unresolved validity and reproducibility issues.

strengths: Significance: Evaluating inappropriate memory use alongside beneficial personalization addresses an important practical problem. The 500-example benchmark and evaluation of 18 models could provide a useful resource for memory-system development.

Originality: The contribution is primarily a new evaluation perspective: combining cross-domain response distortion, memory-induced sycophancy, and beneficial memory use. This usefully extends recall-focused benchmarks without requiring a fundamentally new algorithm.

Soundness: The memory-disabled control provides meaningful evidence of memory amplification: across five models, sycophancy decreases from 59–100% with memory to 19–38% without it (Appendix K). Memory swapping, paraphrasing, alternative system prompts, multi-turn evaluation, and retrieval experiments provide additional supporting evidence.

Presentation: The main paper clearly explains the benchmark structure and distinguishes its three evaluation settings. Extensive qualitative examples and prompt/retrieval mitigation experiments help readers understand the observed behaviors and safety–utility tradeoffs.

Limitations and ethics: Synthetic profiles avoid directly exposing real users' private histories. The manuscript acknowledges synthetic-data limitations and excludes agentic deployments explicitly. No material research-ethics violation is evident.
weaknesses: Construct validity is insufficiently established. The paper claims that sycophancy queries are objective and memories contain clearly false biases, but Appendix Q.2 includes a preference for end-of-day engineering summaries over stand-ups, which is not inherently false. Cross-domain examples are also debatable: Appendix Q.1 treats considering a known deep-water phobia when recommending ocean documentaries as inappropriate. These examples require stronger adjudication of when personalization becomes harmful, rather than assuming that departure from a generic answer is a failure.

The headline rates are not adequately calibrated against judge error. Appendices E.4–E.5 report only about 78% binary agreement with humans; cross-domain precision is 68%, and Figure 12 shows eight false positives among 32 human-acceptable responses. Counting any of three generations as failure can amplify false positives. The bootstrap intervals omit this measurement uncertainty, and strong model-ranking correlations do not establish accurate absolute failure rates. A larger human audit of the actual three-response failure criterion is needed.

The beneficial-memory metric is internally inconsistent. Section 4.3 defines score 1 as success and scores ≥2 as failure, whereas Appendix R.4.3 defines score 3 as success and score 1 as failure; Appendix G also describes score 3 as proper integration. Appendix S's examples follow the opposite convention. This could be an undocumented score transformation, but without clarification and evaluation code, the utility results and safety–utility conclusions cannot be independently checked.

Deployment-risk claims exceed the sampling evidence. Both safety subsets undergo adversarial MCTS search and failure-based selection. The small effect of the subsequent validation filter on sycophancy does not undo the initial adversarial selection. Thus, Section 5.1's claim that sycophancy rates approximate deployment risk is unsupported. Appendix I also assumes independent, representative prompts without establishing this for tree-generated, filtered candidates. The results support a challenging stress test, not population failure prevalence.

Reproducibility remains materially incomplete. Appendix C promises release upon publication, while Appendix R supplies prompt summaries and references external text filenames rather than reproducing the complete prompts in the supplied manuscript. Target-model decoding temperatures, token limits, and complete snapshot identifiers are not consistently specified. The GEPA experiment does not clearly state whether its 60 optimization examples are excluded from evaluation. Appendix C.2.2 also lists MiniMax-M2 in both search and validation, contradicting the claim that validation models were entirely held out.

The evidence establishes susceptibility to supplied profile context more directly than a distinct effect of long-term persistence or forgetting. Memories are externally constructed and injected; extraction, updating, and temporal retention are not evaluated. This is a reasonable scope, but claims about structural long-term-memory mechanisms and when systems should forget should be narrowed accordingly. Overall, the useful benchmark idea and broad experiments do not yet outweigh the unresolved measurement and reproducibility issues.

strengths: Significance: Selective memory use is an important evaluation problem. PersistBench usefully combines cross-domain leakage, sycophancy, and beneficial memory use, preventing indiscriminate memory suppression from appearing universally successful.

Soundness: The evaluation covers 18 models and includes substantial controls: memory removal and swapping, paraphrasing, alternative system prompts, simulated multi-turn conversations, and retrieval interventions. In Appendix K, removing memories reduces sycophancy markedly across five models, supporting the central qualitative finding that injected memories can amplify problematic responses.

Originality: The contribution is primarily a focused benchmark and empirical characterization rather than a new algorithm. Studying stored user beliefs alongside irrelevant personalization provides a useful extension of existing contextual-integrity and sycophancy evaluations.

Presentation and validation: The main paper is clearly organized, and the appendices provide extensive examples, filtering statistics, FR@1–3 results, and human evaluations. Human–automated ranking correlations around −0.89 provide encouraging evidence that the benchmark captures meaningful differences between models. The explicit acknowledgment of synthetic-data limitations is appropriate.
weaknesses: Soundness—construct validity: Several examples undermine the asserted boundary between inappropriate influence and beneficial personalization. Appendix Q treats a remembered fear of deep water as irrelevant to recommending deep-sea documentaries, although it could justify a useful content warning. It also characterizes preferences for asynchronous engineering updates over stand-ups as clearly incorrect beliefs, despite their context dependence. The sycophancy rubric presumes an identifiable incorrect belief and can classify balanced treatment as failure. Stronger independent annotation and explicit reference criteria are needed to distinguish factual distortion, reasonable disagreement, and legitimate personalization.

Soundness—deployment claims exceed the sampling design: Section 5.1 says sycophancy scenarios approximate deployment risk, but samples are explicitly optimized through MCTS to induce failures and filtered using model failures. Appendix C.4 compares pre- and post-validation samples that have already undergone adversarial generation; it therefore does not establish naturalistic prevalence. FR@3 is a valid stress-test metric, but the headline percentages describe at least one failure across three attempts on selected challenges, not ordinary response-level deployment risk. The paper should narrow these claims or provide an independently sampled naturalistic evaluation.

Measurement reliability: Appendix E reports only about 78% binary judge accuracy; cross-domain precision is 68%, with 8 of 32 human-acceptable responses falsely flagged. Such errors materially affect thresholded failure rates and can be amplified by the any-of-three aggregation. Strong model-ranking correlations do not establish calibrated absolute rates. The bootstrap intervals omit annotation uncertainty, and Appendix I assumes independent, representative entries without establishing this for related MCTS descendants. A larger human audit of final aggregated outcomes and threshold-sensitivity analysis are needed.

Reproducibility and internal consistency: Section 4.3 defines beneficial-memory scores as 1=success and 3=failure, whereas Appendix R.4.3 gives the judge the reverse scale. Examples follow the main-text convention, but no conversion is documented. Appendix C.2.2 also lists MiniMax-M2 in both generation and supposedly held-out validation sets. Moreover, the supplied manuscript contains prompt summaries and filename references rather than accessible complete prompts; target-model decoding settings are not specified despite the reproducibility statement. These issues prevent confident reconstruction of the reported measurements.

Mitigation evidence and research reporting: GEPA uses 20 examples per category, while mitigation evaluation uses 50 per category, without establishing that these sets are disjoint or documenting the optimization budget sufficiently. Consequently, the reported safety–utility improvements are not clearly demonstrated on held-out data. Human annotation reporting also omits recruitment, compensation, and consent or oversight details. Synthetic profiles reduce direct privacy concerns, and no material ethical violation is demonstrated, but the human-study reporting should be completed. Overall, the useful benchmark idea and extensive experiments do not yet resolve the validity and reproducibility concerns needed for acceptance.

strengths: Significance: PersistBench addresses a useful gap in memory evaluation: whether assistants should use stored information, rather than merely whether they can recall it. Including 200 cross-domain leakage cases, 200 sycophancy cases, and 100 beneficial-memory cases makes the benchmark relevant to safety–utility trade-offs.

Originality: The contribution is primarily a new evaluation setting and empirical characterization, rather than a new algorithm. Connecting persistent user profiles to response distortion and sycophancy is a meaningful extension of existing contextual-integrity and personalization evaluations.

Soundness: The evaluation covers 18 models and includes substantial supporting experiments: memory-disabled and shuffled-memory controls, paraphrasing, alternative system prompts, simulated multi-turn conversations, and retrieval defenses. In Appendix K, removing memories substantially reduces sycophancy across all five tested models, supporting the narrower claim that these memory sets amplify problematic behavior.

Presentation and validation: The main paper clearly describes the task and construction pipeline, and the appendices provide extensive examples and human validation. Human model preferences correlate strongly with automated rankings. The synthetic-data design limits exposure of real users’ sensitive information, and the limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges synthetic histories and incomplete risk coverage.
weaknesses: Soundness—deployment claims exceed the sampling design. Both safety subsets are explicitly optimized through MCTS to induce failures and filtered using model failures. Nevertheless, Section 5.1 describes sycophancy results as approximating deployment risk. The small change after validation in Appendix C.4 does not remove selection bias already introduced during generation. The results establish vulnerability on an adversarial stress test, not failure prevalence in ordinary use. Appendix I similarly assumes representative, independent samples without adequately addressing shared seeds and adaptive search.

Measurement reliability remains material to the headline rates. Appendix E reports binary judge accuracy of approximately 78%, with cross-domain precision of only 68%. Taking any judged failure across three generations can amplify false positives. Strong human agreement on model rankings does not validate absolute failure rates, and the reported bootstrap intervals do not incorporate judgment uncertainty. A larger, stratified human audit of the final FR@3 decisions and threshold-sensitivity analysis would make the quantitative conclusions more reliable.

The beneficial-memory scoring specification is contradictory. Section 4.3 defines 1 as successful use and 3 as failure, with scores ≥2 counted as failures; Appendix R.4.3 instead defines 3 as perfect and 1 as failure. The examples in Appendix S follow the main-text convention. An undocumented score reversal may explain this, but the manuscript does not establish it. This needs reconciliation because beneficial-memory results support the central safety–utility comparisons.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the supplied submission. Appendix C.1 promises a release upon publication, while Appendix R provides prompt summaries and references full prompt files that are not accessible links or embedded attachments in the PDF. Target-model sampling parameters are also not specified despite the claim that they are. The GEPA optimization/evaluation split is unclear: the paper reports optimization on 20 examples per category and evaluation on 50 per category without establishing disjointness. Appendix C.2 also lists MiniMax-M2 in both sycophancy generation and validation, contradicting the claim that validation models were held out.

Construct validity needs more careful calibration at the personalization boundary. For example, Appendix S.1 labels an otherwise helpful response as a failure because it suggests sharing the user’s creative background when helping a cousin prepare for an art exam. This is plausibly insensitive, but its classification as harmful cross-domain leakage is subjective. Each benchmark item receives only one human verification review, and inter-human ordinal agreement is moderate. Clearer adjudication of borderline cases would strengthen confidence that the benchmark measures inappropriate influence consistently.
